segments.text: I am Dr. Safa Abdo
Executive secretary, Nuclear for Climate I am from Egypt
I want to say a few things.

First, we are sitting here in Kigali, a city that chose to reimagine the future against all odds. That's exactly what we are doing in this session. The question before us today is not whether Africa youth belong to nuclear.
The question is, they are already here. And how we can turn their presence here into lasting impact. NEISA 2026 is a clear signal that Africa is not waiting for invitation.
It is already leading it. And the generation in this room is the center of the future. So our panelists today are living proof of what is possible.
I want real stories from our panelists today, honest answers from each one of them. So let us welcome them. Daniel Ajudeonu
Leadership Team Member and Africa Project Lead, International Student, Young Pugwa
Linnet Nyamweya
President, Kenyan Young Generation in Nuclear
Asmaa Hanafi
Researcher at Alexandria university, Nuclear Engineering and Radiation dept
And finally, Noble Eiaseb
President of African Young Generation in Nuclear (AYGN), Namibia
Welcome all of you. So I will keep it short .
So I will start with you, Daniel. I want to open with you. Your work sits at the intersection of global nuclear policy and African youth leadership.

And I think this is exactly where we should start today. From a global perspective, how can Africa ensure that its nuclear force is not only technically strong but also grounded in ethics, safety culture and responsible leadership? Thank you very much, Safa. And wonderful to see beautiful faces from across Africa.

I've been working with a number of people here remotely and I've seen them today, which is so beautiful. Thank you to the nation for inviting me. I would say that first of all, we must realise that Africa is the future.

I think by 2050, our population is set to get to 850 million youths. We must ask ourselves the question, how do we tap into the potential of these young people to accelerate Africa's clean energy future? Technical competence without ethical grounding is a liability, not an asset. Especially in the nuclear field where safety is critical, safeguards, robust mechanisms are needed.

From our end at Young Pugwash, this is something we are already working on through our African Atomic Policy Lab, which our Secretary General,Karen Hallberg , talked about a few minutes ago. We are training the next generation of African policy experts. We are not just training people who have a background in social science, but we are training engineers, physicists, scientists in nuclear non-proliferation, safety and safeguards, disarmament verification, open source intelligence, research security, policy research, diplomacy and tradecraft, strategic communications, and media advocacy.

Beyond this theoretical and skills-based training, these fellows received one-on-one personalized career mentorship and research supervision from distinguished international and African experts from a range of world-class institutions, including Harvard University, Texas A&M University, the Oak Ridge National Laboratory in the US, the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, to name a few. For me, why this is so profound is because as a young leader in the global nuclear policy space, I've been in circles where African perspectives are highly underrepresented, and I must say that I've also been on panels reviewing applications for young Africans to participate in some of these events, but the quality of the applications and the research outputs had been low. As a result, we've had to prioritize non-Africans, even if we want that inclusivity.

And we are changing this narrative, and I'm glad to be leading it at Pugwash. Also, to add to that, this year we are training 25 young Africans from over 16 African countries, and my goal is that within the next five years, we would have trained over 500 young Africans through this program. What makes it most remarkable is that we are not just training you to learn and produce research, but you have the opportunity to publish your research with reputable international policy outlets, such as the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, European Leadership Network, Insignia, and a whole lot of them.

And the best authors receive cash prizes, and the top author gets a fully funded opportunity to present their paper at an international conference. So, it is very critical that Africa, we begin to think of how we must platform African ideas, African perspectives, and I'm proud to say that at Pugwash, the African Atomic Policy Lab was designed by an African, founded by an African, and it is currently being led by an African theme, contextualized to the African context, and we hope that we continue to deepen our engagement with the African community. Thank you very much.
Thank you very much, Daniel. And I think this framing and the efforts we have done will last with us in the whole conversation today.
So, I will move with Linnet . you have been building this from the ground in Kenya. I think your personal journey speaks directly to what many people in this room are also living right now.

So, please, if you could answer this question, from your personal journey, what are the biggest barriers young Africans face when entering nuclear-related careers, and what has helped you push them through? Okay. Thank you so much, Safa. First of all, I'd like to thank the NEISA 2026 for the invite.
It's my first time in Kigali, and I'm really enjoying my stay. So, I'll just talk a little bit about myself. My experience is, I did my undergrad in chemistry.

I was lucky to have a scholarship by the government of Kenya that I did my master's in nuclear science. I later joined the Nuclear Power and Energy Agency, and then I'm currently doing my specializing master's in nuclear safeguards at the Politecnico di Milano in Italy. And beyond that, I'm the current president of Kenyan Young Generation in Nuclear.

That aside, the barriers that most young Africans will face in this room, firstly, is that our conversations about nuclear are more global than local. So, we haven't yet localized the nuclear talks, whereby we look at what Africa needs, because our needs are not similar to the developed countries' needs. First of all, we have a rising demand in energy, we have a rising population, and we also have urgent needs to have our people connected to the grid, leave alone the industrialization needs that we have.

So, this really makes young people not to know how will they connect their careers to the nuclear, which is really an emerging technology at this point. Also, as much as we go to school and get to study in our universities, we have a problem with integrating what we are learning with the nuclear landscape, because we have labs that are not really well equipped to do the nuclear R&D, or even organizations that are not fully nuclear. So, what that does is, it makes it so difficult for students to clearly see where they will fit in the nuclear ecosystem.

I'm so happy that this conversation is changing, especially with NEISA 2026. We've heard that Africa needs to move urgently within the next five years, we need to strengthen our cooperation, we need to build a common talent pool in Africa, where we are able to share expertise, resources, trainings, and opportunities. Also, we've now realized that you cannot develop nuclear in silos.
We need to come together, create these opportunities for each and every one of us, so that we move forward quicker. Thank you. Thank you very much, Lynette.
Thank you for giving us the solution. And yes, your barriers are real, and I am confident that a lot of people in this room have been through the same situation as yours. Move to you, Aboubakar.

Aboubakar, you are leading the continental network, which means that the level where the individual stories become systems. I want to push on that with you. As a president of IUIGN Africa, how do you see youth networks contributing to a continental nuclear talent pipeline rather than fragmenting country by country? Thank you very much, Safa, for the question.

Youth are very, very important, and that is why, especially in talent development, and everywhere around the globe, you find developed countries using different strategies to attract youth. That's because they are the people that you use when you want to develop a talent. You hardly see positions for postdocs or PhDs being announced for ages around 40s or 50s or 60s.
It is always the youth. And the same thing when it comes to jobs, especially jobs that have to do with tech, mostly it is the youth. And Africa has an enormous pool of that.

This tells you that youth are very, very important. Another thing is, when you talk about technical cooperation, we as a network have been working together since our early days in this field. What that means for the future is, when you talk about technical cooperation, since we have already worked together and synergized with one another, it means later in the future when we become leaders of this industry on this continent, international cooperation will be much easier.

Because like we've heard in several forums, it has been mentioned that if you want to go far, go together. If you want to go fast, go alone. So that we have been developing for quite some time now, and I'm very sure with time it continues to develop.
And that will be something that will definitely help the industry on the continent. Thank you, Abu Bakr. I think you provide us with a continental lens on your perspective as a strategist for IYGM.
Thank you. I'm moving now to Asma. You are a member of Women in Nuclear Young Generation.
Also, you built something from scratch, Green Society. Let me start with you with this question. Networking and visibility are often open doors early in a career.

How can young professionals in nuclear, especially women, build meaningful international connections from where they are right now? Thank you, Safa. It's my first time to be here. For networking and visibility for career growth, there is a lot of things to say.
But let me simplify it into only three words. Discover, learn, lead. When you discover yourself, know what is your weakness point, and how to turn this weakness point into strength point.

How you can have your skills, qualifications, and invest in them. That's how you have self-awareness. Also, this self-confidence is the foundation of building a meaningful connection and learning new skills.
That's about discovery. When we go to the second word, which is learn, you have to learn continuously. Using social media, we spend much time scrolling.

What if we have this time management and learn from experts and scrolling and having new connections with national and international. I have my own methodology, which is think globally and act locally. If you start building something, you have to start by yourself.
Then you can lead. I started Green Society with only my sister. She is a professional visual artist.

From there, when we are moving and seeing how the sea level is rising, I say I have to invest my science and educational background to create something for kids to let them know the climate change consequences and know more about sustainability. Also, using something very interesting to cross boundaries, we are using art. We are using this coloring book we created from scratch to raise awareness and public acceptance, not only for nuclear energy but also for sustainability.

We created, also from scratch, 44 cards. These cards are a board game because now we have to move to interactive learning and using gamification creativity and innovation. We are in the new era of using AI but it depends on how you can use AI.
It also depends on references. If you have AI tools, you have to check from time to time for references from well-trusted websites and knowledge. That's how we can do it.
That's how we can build our networking from our colleagues, friends, even family members. We can do it. Thank you.
Thank you very much, Asmaa. I see you brought your cards with you. Bringing examples is what pushes things forward.
Thank you, Asmaa. I may move now to Nobel. Let's start with you, Nobel.

Your country, Namibia, is the world's top uranium producer and yet no nuclear power plant and imports your own electricity. That's a contrast and a powerful background for your story. Please tell us what inspired your journey into the nuclear sector and how did being part of a youth network shape who you are now as a professional? Thank you very much, Asmaa.
Ladies and gentlemen, Africa is at an inflection point. Africa is pregnant with natural resources. However, the benefits are mostly miscarried.

We need to speak about ensuring how do we bring back this thing called beneficiation within the African shores. I'm an advocate for ensuring why and how Africa must benefit from her resources. Long must be the time where we only export.

We must start bringing our facilities onshore. We must ensure that our people are capacitated and upskilled to be able to take over the industries. We know that Africa is having problems in the health sector.
We have problems in agriculture, water scarcity issues, food security issues. Nuclear comes in here. Nuclear science and technology is something that is very important.

As my moderator said, Namibia is the third largest producer of uranium, the first in Africa. What do we really have to show for that? We are exporting this resource. How do we ensure to change that formula? In my opinion, that formula is wrong.

We cannot be rejoicing for the fact that we are the biggest producer of uranium. To what benefit? How do we ensure that we beneficiate the mineral resources, let's say uranium, within the African shores, within Namibia? I'm a very strong advocate for bringing back mineral beneficiation within our shores. Ensuring that Africans are capacitated, upskilled, and partnerships from international partners come on board.

We need to change this thing where Africans have this mentality of negotiating from a position of weakness. We are not weak. We need to start to learn our strength and we need to start to dictate our terms.

An investment must not come at the detriment of the locals. It should be to the benefit of the locals and the benefits to the investors also. To that I say, when I founded the Young Generation in Nuclear for Namibia and subsequently joined the African Young Generation in Nuclear and the International Youth Nuclear Congress, these entities are very important because it enhances your visibility, it enhances your leadership skills, and also it's very important because it breaks down these proverbial boundaries that we have set for ourselves as Africans.
We are our own worst enemies. People, let's say, look at Europe. They are having borders, but those are basically not borders.
Africa, we are very much about our borders. We need to change that formula. Thank you very much.
Thank you. You shared a lot of feelings and emotions. Thank you.

I will come back to you, Daniel. I want to ask about your work in global governance. What lessons from international scientific cooperation can help African youth move from being just observers of the global nuclear governance to active participants in shaping this? Thank you very much.

This question is close to my heart and I'm going to be very direct. During this year's edition of the African Atomic Policy Lab, the chair of the Pugwash Council, who is also the co-chair of the German Federation of Scientists, delivered a powerful session, a special dialogue, one-on-one with the African young leaders participating in the fellowship. And in his words, I'm paraphrasing, he said, you think you are ignored, but you are not.

And I want to tell every African youth here, Pugwash is here to support scientific cooperation in Africa and we are doing that through the African Atomic Policy Lab already. Also, another dimension to this, some years ago, I published a paper on challenging racism and white supremacy in the nuclear field. I published the paper alongside some of my colleagues from the Global North.

And one of the core recommendations was that Global North countries, particularly those who often host international conferences, should ease visa processes for young Africans and young people from the Global South generally. And I'm proud to say that in recent times, I've seen young Africans, including those from countries sanctioned by the United States, participate at conferences in New York, and I must acknowledge you for that. That is beautiful.

I encourage every other country represented here that hosts conferences, please kindly follow suit. When we have African voices in the room, African perspectives are platformed. They build leadership that enables them to contribute to building Africa's nuclear sector.
They build relationships that fosters the ability to negotiate at the table when they become decision makers. For me, that was scientific cooperation. And I would also go into another dimension now.
I'm speaking with multiple faces. Our voice is our power. I have a proposal to the African government here.

Over time, we've had Africans go to the North to learn. We've had organizations try to support young Africans to do research as much as they can. But now, at NEISA 2026, I want to propose that an African Nuclear Scholars Fellowship be established under which young Africans in the nuclear field, scientists, engineers, including social scientists, are placed in paid salaried positions at reputable institutions across the globe.

We are to conduct scientific research and generate solutions to African and global nuclear challenges. And when they work alongside experts in the field, they gain direct exposure to the operational, policy, and research dimensions of the global nuclear sector. Tell me, when they come back to Africa, we are building our own sector.

And finally, I am going to be a bit vulnerable here. At NEISA 2026, part of the outputs, part of the things that we must look up to, must include African governments supporting talent retention. It's one thing to build capacity through scientific cooperation.
It's another to retain the talent that you have built. We have so many young Africans going to other countries to work. It's time for us to keep them here.

And finally, I would say that, for me, as a young leader, at Pugwash, I work on a voluntary basis. But I'm proud to say that I founded the African Atomic Policy Lab, designed and developed the curriculum, recruited faculty from Africa and other countries of the world, and am currently implementing the 2026 cohort. I said it's not to boast.

I say it because I want African youth to understand that agency does not wait for salary. It starts with an idea and the will to build. Next year, I hope that we will have the first cohort of the African Nuclear Scholars Fellowship.

And I hope that the young minds here can put their entrepreneurial instincts to work, build something for Africa, and hopefully, nuclear technology startups that may not build reactors, but softwares such as those to track nuclear materials and to enhance safety and monitoring systems. In the next 20 years, if we do this, Africa can become the hub for nuclear entrepreneurship, and Africa's nuclear sector will be booming. Thank you very much.
Thank you very much, Daniel. I kindly ask the governors here in this room to listen to him. This is an actionable roadmap.
And to students, to write it down. Thank you, Daniel. So I will move to Linnet .

And please, I will come back to you with something. I want you to provide this room with something more hands-on for the students and tell them what practical steps can students and young professionals take today to position themselves in the sector that is still emerging across much of this continent. Okay.

Thank you so much, Safa, again, for the chance to answer this. So at KYGN, first of all, we work with a lot of students from high schools to universities. We launch nuclear clubs in high schools and also launch chapters for KYGN in universities.

That's notwithstanding, we also do a lot of mentorship. And one of the things that we keep on encouraging our students to do is to have a strong foundation in whatever they're majoring in. We've heard here today that nuclear power is multidisciplinary.

And that means it's not for scientists and engineers only. It has the social science aspect of it. It's expecting communicators to be in nuclear and because of that, you need to really put a strong foundation in your major.

And also, whatever you're majoring in, you should be able to intersect it with emerging technologies. We now have AI, robotics, cyber security, and all the advanced digital systems that you are getting. Secondly, I urge students to actively seek opportunities outside the classroom.

That means coming to NEISA 2026, that is one of the steps to ensure that you're not staying in the classroom. Another one is attending webinars, going to more conferences. And above all, please join the NEISA club if you're in Rwanda or other various African countries.

We have these chapters where you'll be able to network, increase your visibility, and build your confidence in this field. And above all, you'll be able to connect with professionals in Africa and also globally. I also encourage you guys to have long-term thinking because nuclear projects are long-term.

They are 100 years of preparation and from preparation to decommissioning. So when you look at that, you need to start building your mindset in terms of, are you building your skills okay? Are you continuously learning? And also, are you having the practical exposure that you need? Because every industry needs an X factor and the X factor will be something that will make you be where you're supposed to be in the years to come. And have a thinking that you are going to be the professionals of our future.

Not only today, but the future is coming maybe 10, 15, 20 years. You are the people who are needed to work in these nuclear facilities. So ensure that you build your professional skills from now onwards until you get that job.
, Abubakar Sadiq Aliy
Thank you. Thank you very much. And I hope our students here and our youth absorb your advices.
They are precious. Thank you. So going back to you Abubakar Sadiq Aliy , and please, I want specific, this time with you, I want specific answers.

What concrete initiatives in IYGN are advancing to ensure that young professionals are not only trained, but also given real roles in projects and decision-making spaces? Yes, thank you. This is a very important question and it's very concerning because we are talking about jobs now, placement. And as a past experience, the very moment I picked interest in nuclear science, that was back in high school, the first thing my mentors and my parents asked me was, what are you going to do after you finish this degree? Well, I didn't know because at that time, I didn't even know about the Nigerian Atomic Energy Commission.
5. I didn't know anything. It was just by faith.
And I said, I maintain my stand and I wanted to do that. And they allowed me. So at IYGN, what we do is, of course, you know, we are not a governmental body.

So the highest we do is talk to these organisations or governmental bodies. But then we do things like trying to make sure that our members upgrade their skills. Because when they upgrade their skills, that will put them at the forefront in terms of job opportunities and what have you.

And how do we do that? Recently, we sat down and thought, many people do graduate with PhDs, Masters and what have you. But then when it comes to practical skills, in terms of know-how, be it technical know-how in terms of deployment, be it financial understanding of how these things have been done, and a lot of things. And we decided to come up with an initiative which is the Nuclear Science and Technology Innovation Bootcamp.

That way, we intend to bring young people from across the continent to a particular country which has a good technical know-how of the industry. For example, South Africa. In order to get them acclimatised to some of these things, it's going to be a programme of two weeks where they learn some of these skills.
That's another way of doing it. Another way is we encourage members to develop projects. And we try to identify grants that we can align those projects with.

It's an initiative we started earlier this year. And so far, we have members applied for a particular project and we are working on another project. We found some grant applications and we hope this project will be able to be funded by these grants.

And then another thing is we find we try to also put up some initiatives like the African Nuclear Future Initiative. This initiative not only provides permanent jobs but then we tend to look at fellowships, leadership training courses and what have you. What these initiatives do is to keep the members busy without thinking, we don't have anything to do.

So it makes them do something and they are also learning. So whenever the opportunities pop up, they are ready and they will just grab them instead of sitting without doing nothing. And then another thing is also we try to make sure to encourage them to apply for internships and all that.

Even if they are not being paid. Just like Daniel mentioned, he was doing a voluntary role and then on the role he has done so many projects, that will make him develop skills and even find opportunities that will probably lead him to jobs and what have you. So these are some of the initiatives we put down.

I think the last thing we do is try to work with governmental bodies and also especially the IEA to look into creating some opportunities. For example, I know the United States do, other countries do but the United States do most, the JPO program trying to encourage governmental bodies to also follow through that route. It's a program whereby the government pays your job and then you work with the IEA and then probably after three years you'll be released.
That could probably give you opportunities for international placements and what have you. So these are some of the few things we try to put in place. Thank you very much Safa for the question.

Thank you Abubakar for bringing up all the examples of the great job you've done and hopefully it will continue in the future on a larger scale. So I will come back to you Noble and I want to come back to you with a question and this time in your network. How can youth networks do a better job of connecting students with mentors and institutions and international opportunities and what is IYG in Namibia doing differently to make that happen? Thank you.

Before I go, first of all I would like to take the opportunity to thank His Excellency Paul Kagame and the esteemed government of Rwanda for making this possible. The great people at the Rwanda Atomic Energy Board, RURA and also the NEISA Secretariat. You don't understand how important it is to involve youth from all over Africa to summit here.

It is very commentable and I'm very grateful for that. So in my opinion it is very, very important that we enhance the mentorship systems. So as the previous speakers were saying you need to create a relationship with a possible person that you want to mentor you create that relationship and get in a situation where you have a mentorship program. So for various YGNs you would basically have a mentorship program where you also identify as a YGN who are the key players, who are the key stakeholders in your country. And one thing that I always say is I don't like this thing of borders.

So I call it the proverbial African borders. So you can identify somebody that is sitting in Zambia, Zimbabwe, South Africa, Egypt, Morocco. You don't necessarily have to be just because you're a Namibian you just want a Namibian mentor.

Identify somebody that is outside your country. Identify somebody that is even in Europe, in the Americas, in China, so forth. So create strong mentorship programs and then also it is important knowing that most of the YGNs are non-governmental institutions.

It is very, very important that you create partnerships. Whether that is now with your BRICS nuclear platform, whether that is now with your CNNC, whether that is now with your local regulators, whether that is with your uranium producers, your mining experts, mining stakeholders. Whether that is now let's say with the IAEA because you need to have direct communication with the people that are actually making decisions.

And one thing that I'm imploring the government officials that are in this room and people that are in higher positions is please break the red tape. Break the red tape and create a situation where you capacitate the young people of your country, you ensure that the young people are able to actually go. I had a very, very strange meeting the other day and it sparked something in my mind.

We went to RURA and the way these people are treating the Rwanda young generation in nuclear, it was amazing. They have an open door policy for the young generation in Rwanda. We want more governments to come on board like that.

It is important that we break the bottlenecks. It is important that we ensure that the young people, I don't like this thing that we are saying the young people are the future. No, we are not the future.
We are the current. We want to take charge of the future.

Partnerships are very important with your various institutions, universities, academia, and also ensure that you are visible. You don't necessarily have to be paid at the beginning, of course. We all like money, but at the beginning, volunteer if you need to volunteer.

Create mechanisms where your network has an ability to say, for example, we are going to send somebody to volunteer this time. We are going to send somebody to volunteer. You are creating awareness and you are also creating an education corridor that is building synergy within various entities.
Also, inclusion. Very, very important. Ladies and gentlemen, and I go back to the officials and the important people.
We are all important, but some of you are sitting at the right tables. When you are sitting at the right tables, please ensure that you include a youth. You are having a ministerial meeting.

You are talking about the future of your country, but you are not involving the people that are the future of your country. Does it make sense? Make it make sense. Involve somebody from your country, a young generation.

Bring the people on board. If you are having an IAEA meeting, let there be a young person that is able to ensure that the young person's voice and opinion is heard. Because you know for sure that the young people, our opinions are very, very varied.
We want things done in a certain way. Now you are making decisions for us, for our future, without our presence. It does not make sense.
Please fix that. Lastly, engagement is very, very important. I would give credence to our president Paul Kagame , for ensuring that we are always a united continent.
There is synergy that is being built. We are ensuring that the nations where there are no YGNs are coming on board. It is important that we ensure we are engaging throughout Africa.
Not only that, we are breaking and closing ourselves as Africa. We want to involve Europe. We want to involve the Americas.
We want to involve the Asians. Breaking that and engaging. That is very, very important.
Thank you very much. Thank you, Noble. Thank you very much.
I just want to stress on two very important points you provided here. The first one, volunteer. Don't wait for immediate reward.
Volunteer. Start by volunteering. The second thing, enlarge your scope.
Me, myself, all my mentors are not Egyptian. They are from another country. Please, gentlemen, let me finish with a personal story.

Last year, in Brazil, an African woman delegate came to our booth and she pulled me aside and she said, while I was promoting nuclear energy as a clean source of energy, she said, stop, don't do that. Don't promote nuclear energy because we are in Africa and are not ready yet for this technology. After this session, I think I have an answer for her.
I don't know. Somehow, I hope she can hear me. I want to say, no, Africa is ready.
Thank you.
